name: Stonehenge

phases.label: Circular ditch, bank and cremation cemetery
Sarsen circle, trilithons and bluestones
Standing monument, no longer rebuilt
Standing remains on open downland, visited in the Roman period
phases.note: AD 43 is an era boundary only: English Heritage says Stonehenge was frequently visited in the Roman period and records no destruction at the conquest. When individual stones fell or were taken is generally unknown.

summary: The ditch and bank were dug about 3000 BCE and the great stones set up about 2500 BCE. The bluestones were rearranged two or three centuries later and the last known digging, the Y and Z holes, dates to 1800-1500 BCE.
uncertainty: Phase boundaries are rounded radiocarbon estimates. How long it stayed in active use after 1500 BCE is not known.

name: Durrington Walls

phases.label: Short-lived settlement of the Stonehenge builders
phases.note: English Heritage: occupied for a relatively short time between 2580 and 2470 BCE. The 2550-2451 span is a display window for that bracket, not a century of continuous occupation.

phases.label: Great henge earthwork
Earthwork, out of use

summary: A very large late Neolithic settlement beside the Avon, later enclosed by Britain's largest henge. It is linked to the building of the sarsen phase at Stonehenge, 3 km away.
uncertainty: Dates are rounded from memory of the Stonehenge Riverside Project results (settlement about 2500 BCE, in use for only a few decades). Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Avebury

phases.label: Henge and stone circles under construction
Henge and avenues in use
Abandoned monument; a village grows inside it in the Middle Ages

summary: The largest stone circle in Britain, inside a huge henge ditch, built and altered from about 2850 to about 2200 BCE. Its monuments were abandoned around 1800 BCE.
uncertainty: Internal sequence of the circles and avenues is not closely dated.

name: Silbury Hill

phases.label: Mound built within this dating window
phases.note: English Heritage: probably built over a short period between about 2470 and 2350 BCE, though enlarged over several generations rather than in one campaign. The phase spans the dating bracket; it is not a measured 120-year building schedule.

phases.label: Completed mound; a Roman roadside settlement later lay at its foot

summary: The largest artificial prehistoric mound in Europe, probably raised over a short period between about 2470 and 2350 BCE. Its purpose is unknown.
uncertainty: No burial has been found; the function is a matter of conjecture.

name: West Kennet Long Barrow

phases.label: Chambered tomb in use
Sealed tomb

summary: One of the largest Neolithic chambered tombs in Britain, built around 3650 BCE, used for at least a thousand years and blocked with great sarsens around 2000 BCE.
uncertainty: Construction date is a modelled radiocarbon estimate; the date of final blocking is approximate. Dates are English Heritage's round figures.

name: Windmill Hill

phases.label: Causewayed enclosure, a seasonal gathering place
Earthwork, out of use

summary: The largest known Neolithic causewayed enclosure, three rings of interrupted ditch on a low hill near Avebury.
uncertainty: Start date is a modelled estimate; the length of use is uncertain. Dates are English Heritage's figures: built around 3675 BCE, in use until around 2500 BCE, largely abandoned by the end of the third millennium.

name: Hambledon Hill

phases.label: Neolithic causewayed enclosure complex
Out of use
Iron Age hillfort
Hillfort largely abandoned

summary: A chalk spur in Dorset used twice: as a large early Neolithic enclosure complex and, three thousand years later, as a multivallate hillfort.
uncertainty: Both date ranges are approximate; the end of Iron Age occupation is not well fixed. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Cissbury

phases.label: Neolithic flint mines
Mines disused
Large Iron Age hillfort
Hillfort abandoned; interior later ploughed

summary: Among the earliest flint mines in Britain, with over 200 shafts on the South Downs, later enclosed by one of the largest hillforts in Sussex.
uncertainty: The mines began around or soon after 4000 BCE; all four dates are rounded. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Langdale axe quarries

phases.label: Stone axe quarries on Pike of Stickle
Quarries disused

summary: High fell-side quarries whose green volcanic stone was made into polished axes found all over Britain.
uncertainty: Date range is approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Castlerigg

phases.label: Stone circle
Standing monument

summary: A ring of 38 stones among the Lake District fells, probably raised in the late Neolithic.
uncertainty: Never securely dated by excavation. English Heritage puts it at about 4,500 years ago; Aubrey Burl's case for about 3200 BCE, which would make it one of the earliest circles in Britain, is described there as not strongly supported.

name: Thornborough Henges

phases.label: Three aligned henges
Earthworks; early Bronze Age burial place
phases.note: English Heritage: burial continued around the henges in the early Bronze Age (about 2400-1500 BCE), with round barrows; 2000 BCE is a display boundary, not the end of use.

summary: Three large henges in a line across the Ure-Swale plain, the largest ritual complex between the Thames and Orkney.
uncertainty: Not closely dated. English Heritage says the three henges were built about 4,500 to 5,000 years ago, over an older cursus, and stayed a focus for burials into the early Bronze Age (a nearby timber row is put at 1800-1600 BCE). The end date here is a judgement.

name: Arbor Low

phases.label: Henge with a circle of limestone slabs
Standing monument

summary: A henge and recumbent stone circle on the White Peak limestone plateau.
uncertainty: Not closely dated. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Grime's Graves

phases.label: Deep galleried flint mines worked
phases.note: Healy et al. 2018: the deep galleried shafts were worked probably from the third quarter of the 27th century BCE until the decades around 2400 BCE.

phases.label: Shallower pits in the west of the site
phases.note: Healy et al. 2018: shallow pits continued for perhaps three centuries after the galleried shafts went out of use; the end year is approximate.

phases.label: Mines disused; mining briefly resumed about 1550-1450 BCE, then middens and a settlement from about 1400 BCE
Iron Age burial ground
Hollows in heathland; a hundred meeting place from about 939

summary: A field of more than 400 late Neolithic flint mine shafts in the Norfolk Breckland. The deep galleried shafts were worked from about 2650 to about 2400 BCE and shallower pits for perhaps three centuries more; mining resumed briefly in the mid 2nd millennium BCE.

name: Holme timber circle (Seahenge)

phases.label: Timber circle around an upturned oak

summary: A ring of 55 split oak posts around an inverted tree stump, built on a saltmarsh. Tree rings show the timbers were felled in 2049 BCE.
uncertainty: The felling date is precise; how long the circle was used is unknown, so the end date is nominal. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Flag Fen

phases.label: Timber causeway and platform being built
Causeway used for offerings of metalwork

summary: A kilometre-long post alignment and timber platform across the fen edge near Peterborough, built in stages between about 1365 and 967 BCE and used for ritual deposits long afterwards.
uncertainty: End of use is approximate (deposits continued for more than 1,200 years in all). Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Must Farm

phases.label: Pile-dwelling settlement, burned within about a year

summary: A small late Bronze Age settlement of round houses on stilts over a fen channel, destroyed by fire very soon after it was built and preserved in the silt.
uncertainty: Built about 850 BCE; the year is approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Grimspound

phases.label: Walled Bronze Age settlement of 24 round houses
Surviving settlement remains; end of occupation uncertain
phases.note: 800 BCE is the end of English Heritage's conventional range, not a dated abandonment. How long it was used is unknown; English Heritage links the decline of upland settlement from about 1000 BCE to soil erosion after clearance, not to a dated climatic event.

summary: The best-known of the Bronze Age enclosed settlements on Dartmoor, part of a moor then divided by long field boundaries (reaves).
uncertainty: Never dated by modern excavation; the range is the conventional one. English Heritage gives 'probably late Bronze Age (about 1500-800 BC)' and notes the settlement pattern was changing by about 1000 BCE; there is still no radiocarbon date.

name: Uffington White Horse and Castle

phases.label: Chalk-cut horse
Horse and hillfort
Hill figure, kept scoured

summary: A 110 m stylised horse cut into the chalk of the Berkshire Downs, with an early Iron Age hillfort on the ridge above.
uncertainty: English Heritage reports the horse as dated to the later Bronze Age or Iron Age, between 1740 and 210 BCE; the start date used here sits inside that bracket and is not a measurement. The hillfort's 700 BCE start is from memory.

name: Maiden Castle

Deserted earthworks

summary: One of the largest hillforts in Britain (Ham Hill in Somerset is larger, at 84 ha). In the middle Iron Age (about 400-120 BCE) it was the main settlement of southern Dorset; by the Roman invasion it was almost empty.
uncertainty: The story of a Roman assault in 44 CE is now questioned. The end of the temple is not dated; 430 is nominal.

name: Danebury

phases.label: Early hillfort
Developed hillfort, densely occupied
Reduced to a single farm
Earthworks

summary: The most thoroughly excavated hillfort in Britain, with streets of round houses and thousands of grain storage pits; perhaps 200-350 people lived inside.
uncertainty: Population is an excavator's estimate. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Cadbury Castle

name: Glastonbury Lake Village

phases.label: Iron Age village on an artificial island
Abandoned to rising water

summary: A waterlogged Iron Age village in the Somerset Levels, exceptionally well preserved.
uncertainty: Date range approximate. Not checked against a fetched source: dates and size come from general reference knowledge.

name: Hengistbury Head

phases.label: Promontory settlement behind the Double Dykes
Cross-Channel trading port
Trade falls away after Caesar's Gallic wars
Minor occupation

summary: The main known port of late Iron Age Britain before Caesar: Italian wine, glass and figs came in, and metals went out to Armorica.
uncertainty: The peak is inferred from wine amphorae, most of which predate 50 BCE. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Stanwick

phases.label: Vast earthwork enclosure of the Brigantes
Abandoned after the Roman conquest of the north

summary: Some 300 hectares of earthworks in North Yorkshire, probably the seat of the Brigantian rulers who were clients of Rome until about 69 CE.
uncertainty: The link to Queen Cartimandua is an inference; dates are approximate. English Heritage dates the ramparts to the 1st century CE, with occupation from the middle of the century and decline after 70; the start year 40 is approximate.

name: London

Tudor London
Jacobean London, roughly 200,000 people or more

summary: Founded about 47-50 CE, burned in 60/61, the largest town of Roman Britain, then almost deserted for two centuries. From the late 9th century it grew back inside its Roman walls and by 1377 had about three times as many taxpayers as any other English town.
uncertainty: Sizes are relative ranks, not populations. Descend into the London site for dated, sourced detail. Roman dates checked against the London Museum timeline (founded 47-50, burned 60-61, wall 200-220, end 400-410) and English Heritage (founded about 50, wall about 200). Post-Roman dates and all sizes still rest on Wikipedia and judgement.

name: Colchester

name: St Albans

phases.label: Verlamion, a centre of the Catuvellauni

Late Roman Verulamium

Market town; abbey dissolved 1539

summary: The third great town of Roman Britain by tradition, burned by Boudica in 61. The medieval abbey and town grew on the hill outside the Roman walls, around the supposed grave of Britain's first martyr.
uncertainty: Roman occupation ended between about 400 and 450. The abbey's foundation by Offa about 793 is a later tradition. English Heritage confirms the Boudican destruction about 60 and a town wall built 265-270. Other dates, including Offa's foundation of the abbey (a later tradition), are supported only by Wikipedia.

name: York

phases.label: Eboracum, legionary fortress of the Ninth, then the Sixth Legion

Northern capital under English earls, then Norman castles and minster
Late medieval and Tudor York, seat of the Council of the North

summary: Founded as a legionary fortress in 71. Two emperors died here and Constantine was proclaimed here in 306. It was the Viking capital of the north from 866/7 to 954 and the second town of England in 1377.
uncertainty: The 5th and 6th centuries are almost blank. York had slipped to about fifteenth by wealth in the 1520s. 71, 627, 735, 866 and 954 are confirmed by VCH City of York, which attributes the colonia to Severus. Later rankings follow tax tables reported on Wikipedia.

name: Lincoln

Danish borough, one of the Five Boroughs
Norman castle and cathedral; a leading wool town
Declining cloth town
Much decayed city

summary: A fortress of about 60 CE turned into a colonia for veterans, probably in 86. It revived under Danish rule and stood among the four or five largest English towns from Domesday to the 13th century.
uncertainty: The colonia date is the favoured estimate, not a recorded one. Whether Lincoln was a 4th-century provincial capital is debated. The move of the see to Lincoln in 1072 is confirmed by English Heritage. Roman and Danish dates are supported only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Gloucester

phases.label: Forts at the Severn crossing (Kingsholm)

Minster of St Peter; later a Mercian burh
Refounded burh of Aethelflaed; royal crown-wearing place
Cathedral city and river port

summary: A colonia founded under Nerva at the lowest crossing of the Severn. It was eighth by Russell's Domesday estimate and seventeenth in 1377.
uncertainty: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's capture of Gloucester in 577 is a late and doubtful record. The 679 and c. 900 dates are from memory. The minster of about 679-81, Aethelflaed's refoundation (fortified by 902-14, St Oswald's by 909) and the see of 1541 are from VCH Gloucester. Roman dates are supported only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Chester

Cathedral city; the Dee is silting

summary: Begun in the mid 70s as the largest legionary fortress in Britain and held until the late 4th or early 5th century. Refortified in 907, it became the seat of a Norman marcher earldom.
uncertainty: The date of the legion's departure is not known. 74, about 90 and 907 are from VCH Cheshire; 1071 for the earldom is from memory.

name: Wroxeter

phases.label: Fort, then legionary fortress
Viroconium Cornoviorum, civitas capital
Forum partly abandoned, baths decaying
City centre abandoned; small settlement by the ford
phases.note: English Heritage: the city centre had been abandoned by the mid 5th century, but a community continued near the ford. 451 is a display boundary for the centre, not the end of Wroxeter.

summary: Founded as a military base about 47 and refounded as a city in the 90s. At 78 hectares it was one of the largest cities of Roman Britain. Most of the Roman city was never built over, but a small community stayed on by the river ford, where the village and St Andrew's church now stand.
uncertainty: The centre was abandoned by the mid 5th century; claims of grand timber rebuilding into the 6th or 7th century are now doubted.

name: Silchester

phases.label: Calleva, oppidum of the Atrebates
Calleva Atrebatum, civitas capital, walled about 200
Town dwindling
Abandoned; walls stand around open fields

summary: An Iron Age centre founded about 20-10 BCE which became a Roman town and, unusually, was never reoccupied.
uncertainty: English Heritage puts the abandonment 'sometime between AD 550 and 650'; 600 is the midpoint.

name: Richborough

phases.label: Invasion bridgehead and supply base
Rutupiae, port town with a 25 m monumental arch

summary: Widely believed to be the landing place of 43 CE and long the formal gateway to Britain. The town was cleared after 250 for a fort, rebuilt in stone in 275-290.
uncertainty: The arch is dated only to between 85 and 150. Coins show activity into the early 5th century.

name: Canterbury

summary: Roman capital of Kent, then from 597 the centre of the English church. It was fourteenth in the 1377 poll tax and tenth by wealth in the 1520s.
uncertainty: How much life continued inside the walls between about 420 and 597 is disputed. St Augustine's Abbey was dissolved in 1538 (from memory). 597-8 (English Heritage, St Augustine's), Becket's murder in 1170 and the end of the priory in 1540 (VCH Kent) are confirmed. Roman dates are supported only by Wikipedia.

name: Winchester

uncertainty: Domesday omits Winchester, so its 11th-century size is an estimate (about 6,000). The 880 date for the replanning is approximate. VCH Hampshire gives the Old Minster's foundation as 643 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle) or 639 (Winchester Annals); 648 here follows another Chronicle reading. Other dates are supported only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

Abbey and wool town

summary: Civitas capital of the Dobunni and, on the usual reconstruction, capital of the 4th-century province of Britannia Prima.
uncertainty: Its role as a provincial capital is an inference from one inscription. English Heritage dates the amphitheatre to the early 2nd century and notes the Chronicle's capture of 577. Other dates are supported only by Wikipedia.

name: Bath

Minster and burh
Cathedral priory and small cloth town
Small spa town

summary: A sanctuary and bathing complex around the hot spring, not an ordinary town. The Roman Baths' own timeline has the buildings collapsing by about 500 and a Saxon church founded in 675.
uncertainty: The temple is usually dated to the 60s-70s; the museum timeline only says the Romans came to Bath about 50. VCH Somerset dates the nunnery charter to 676, a year later than the museum timeline, and puts the bishop's move to Bath in 1088.

name: Exeter

uncertainty: Fortress and town dates are rounded from memory. Rankings are from tax records, which measure taxpayers or wealth. Dates are supported here only by Wikipedia, which is a lead rather than verification.

name: Leicester

name: Battle of Ellendun

phases.label: Battle of Ellendun

name: Battle of Brunanburh

phases.label: Battle of Brunanburh

summary: Aethelstan defeated the allied kings of Dublin, Scotland and Strathclyde, securing the new kingdom of the English.
uncertainty: The location is unknown: over forty sites have been proposed. The marker is at Bromborough on the Wirral, the most widely supported candidate. Date (late 937) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as unlocated.

name: Battle of Maldon

phases.label: Battle of Maldon

summary: Ealdorman Byrhtnoth of Essex was killed fighting a Viking fleet on 10 or 11 August 991; payments of tribute followed.
uncertainty: The causeway to Northey Island fits the Old English poem best but is not proven. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Maldon 991' (list entry 1000019).

name: Battle of Brentford

phases.label: Battle of Brentford

summary: Edmund Ironside crossed the Thames at Brentford two days after relieving London and drove Cnut's army off, at heavy cost to his own men.
uncertainty: Known mainly from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (1016: the king 'went over at Brentford', fought and put the enemy to flight, many English drowning); the exact ground and the month are uncertain.

name: Battle of Assandun

phases.label: Battle of Assandun

summary: On 18 October 1016 Cnut defeated Edmund Ironside; Edmund died weeks later and Cnut took the whole kingdom.
uncertainty: Either Ashingdon (shown) or Ashdon, both in Essex; the question is open. Date (18 October 1016) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as unlocated.

name: Battle of Fulford

phases.label: Battle of Fulford

summary: On 20 September 1066 Harald Hardrada and Tostig defeated the northern earls Edwin and Morcar outside York.
uncertainty: The exact field is disputed. Date (20 September 1066) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as approximately located around Germany Beck and Fulford Ings.

name: Battle of Stamford Bridge

phases.label: Battle of Stamford Bridge

summary: On 25 September 1066 Harold Godwinson surprised and killed Harald Hardrada and Tostig.
uncertainty: Date (25 September 1066) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as different interpretations of where the battle was fought have been suggested. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Stamford Bridge 1066' (list entry 1000035).

name: Battle of Hastings

phases.label: Battle of Hastings

summary: On 14 October 1066 William of Normandy defeated and killed King Harold. Battle Abbey was founded on the site about 1071.
uncertainty: Date (14 October 1066) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as probably accurately located in the fields south of Battle Abbey. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Hastings 1066' (list entry 1000013).

name: Battle of the Standard

phases.label: Battle of the Standard

summary: On 22 August 1138 a northern English army raised by Archbishop Thurstan defeated David I of Scotland near Northallerton.
uncertainty: Date (22 August 1138) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as probably accurately located north of Northallerton. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Northallerton 1138' (list entry 1000027).

name: Battle of Lewes

phases.label: Battle of Lewes

summary: Simon de Montfort captured Henry III and the Lord Edward on 14 May 1264 and ruled in the king's name for a year.
uncertainty: The date, 14 May 1264, is secure. The Battlefields Trust places the battle on the north side of the town but says it is uncertain exactly where between the top of Offham Hill and the medieval town it was fought; the marker is a reference point, not a surveyed battle centre. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Lewes 1264' (list entry 1000018).

name: Battle of Evesham

phases.label: Battle of Evesham

summary: The Lord Edward trapped and killed Simon de Montfort on 4 August 1265.
uncertainty: Date (4 August 1265) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as approximately located on Greenhill north of Evesham. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Evesham 1265' (list entry 1000010).

name: Battle of Neville's Cross

phases.label: Battle of Neville's Cross

summary: A northern English army defeated and captured David II of Scotland outside Durham on 17 October 1346.
uncertainty: Date (17 October 1346) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as accurately located north of Neville's Cross. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Neville's Cross 1346' (list entry 1000024).

name: Battle of Otterburn

phases.label: Battle of Otterburn

summary: A Scottish raiding army defeated the Percys in a moonlit fight in Redesdale.
uncertainty: The exact site is debated. Date (5 August 1388) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as approximately located north-west of Otterburn village. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Otterburn 1388' (list entry 1000029). Chroniclers disagree on the day (5 or 19 August).

name: Battle of Shrewsbury

phases.label: Battle of Shrewsbury

summary: Henry IV defeated the Percy rebellion and Henry 'Hotspur' Percy was killed, on 21 July 1403.
uncertainty: Date (21 July 1403) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as securely located west of St Mary Magdalene's church at Battlefield. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Shrewsbury 1403' (list entry 1000033).

name: First Battle of St Albans

phases.label: First Battle of St Albans

summary: A street fight on 22 May 1455 in which Richard of York captured Henry VI; usually counted as the opening of the Wars of the Roses.
uncertainty: Date (22 May 1455) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as securely located among the streets of the city centre.

name: Battle of Towton

phases.label: Battle of Towton

summary: Fought in snow on Palm Sunday, 29 March 1461. Edward IV's victory secured him the throne; it is often called the largest and bloodiest battle on English soil.
uncertainty: Army sizes (50,000-65,000 combined) and casualty figures are chroniclers' estimates. Date (29 March 1461) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as securely located between Saxton and Towton. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Towton, 1461' (list entry 1000040).

name: Battle of Barnet

phases.label: Battle of Barnet

summary: On Easter Sunday, 14 April 1471, Edward IV defeated and killed Warwick 'the Kingmaker' in fog north of Barnet.
uncertainty: The battlefield lies somewhere between about 800 and 1,600 m north of Barnet; surveys have not yet fixed it. Date (14 April 1471) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as north of Barnet, but not yet precisely located. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Barnet 1471' (list entry 1000001). The marker (Hadley Highstone) is 0.37 km north of the centroid of the registered battlefield and was left where it is, between the two candidate areas.

name: Battle of Tewkesbury

phases.label: Battle of Tewkesbury

summary: On 4 May 1471 Edward IV destroyed the last Lancastrian army; Edward, Prince of Wales, was killed.
uncertainty: Date (4 May 1471) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as securely located south of Tewkesbury. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Tewkesbury 1471' (list entry 1000039).

name: Battle of Bosworth

phases.label: Battle of Bosworth

summary: On 22 August 1485 Henry Tudor defeated Richard III, the last English king to die in battle.
uncertainty: Survey finds published in 2009-10 moved the fighting about 3 km south-west of the traditional site on Ambion Hill. The marker now sits at the Battlefields Trust's grid reference in the Fenn Lanes area, inside the enlarged registered battlefield; it is a reference point, not a surveyed centre. Date (22 August 1485) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Bosworth (Field) 1485' (list entry 1000004).

name: Battle of Stoke Field

phases.label: Battle of Stoke Field

summary: Henry VII defeated the Yorkist army backing Lambert Simnel on 16 June 1487, the last battle of the Wars of the Roses.
uncertainty: Date (16 June 1487) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as approximately located west of East Stoke. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Stoke (Field) 1487' (list entry 1000036).

name: Battle of Flodden

phases.label: Battle of Flodden

summary: On 9 September 1513 the Earl of Surrey defeated a Scottish invasion; James IV and much of the Scottish nobility were killed.
uncertainty: Date (9 September 1513) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as securely located in the fields south of Branxton. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Flodden 1513' (list entry 1000011).
